title: Don’t Fall for the PR Answer
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that the first answer an interviewee gives is almost always the safe, socially acceptable one, and that real insight sits several layers deeper. Drawing on years of consulting interviews, she lays out a five-layer model running from the PR answer to the deep insight. She names why interviewers settle for surface answers: fear of awkwardness, the clock, note-taking instead of listening, and mistaking data for insight. She then offers five follow-up moves (get specific, granular, curious, hypothetical, and quiet) and a list of cues for when to push and when to pivot. The piece closes by reframing the interviewer's job as making truth-telling feel safer than the alternative. Filed under Leadership because the argument is about listening, probing questions and conversational skill with senior people.
points: Most conversations stop at layer one or two, while the useful material lives in layers three to five: actual events, real feelings and deepest concerns.
Interviewers accept surface answers for human reasons (awkwardness, time pressure, distracted note-taking), so the fix is a habit rather than a script.
Five follow-up moves (specific, granular, curious, hypothetical, quiet) each work by lowering defensiveness and inviting detail.
Vague evaluations, minimising words, passive voice and emotional flatness are cues to dig; distress, confidentiality limits and a dry well are cues to pivot.
People withhold the truth because they are human, not deceptive, so the listener's task is to make honesty feel safe.
quotes: Many interviews never get past the first layer (socially acceptable answers). Good interviews reach layer two (comfortable sharing). But the magic - the insights that change how you understand a problem - lives in layers three through five (actual events, real feelings and deepest concerns).
We're afraid of awkwardness. Pushing past someone's first answer feels uncomfortable. What if they think we're prying?
Specificity bypasses the part of their brain that creates polish. When someone recreates a specific moment, they can't help but include the messy details.
Contradictions aren't lies - they might just be incomplete truths. Exploring them reveals complexity.
Hypotheticals create psychological distance. It's easier to be critical about imaginary scenarios than real ones.
Most people can't stand silence. They'll fill it, and what they fill it with is usually more honest than their first answer.
Here's what I've learned: people don't withhold the truth because they're deceptive. They withhold it because they're human. They're protecting themselves, their colleagues, their companies.
